title: Law Enforcement Mental Health and Wellness Act of 2017
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the House on November 28, 2017. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Law Enforcement Mental Health and Wellness Act of 2017

(Sec. 2) This bill directs the Department of Justice (DOJ) to report on Department of Defense and Department of Veterans Affairs mental health practices and services that could be adopted by law enforcement agencies.

Additionally, DOJ's Office of Community Oriented Policing Services must report on programs to address the psychological health and well-being of law enforcement officers.

The bill amends the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 to expand the allowable use of grant funds under the Community Oriented Policing Services program to include establishing peer mentoring mental health and wellness pilot programs within state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies.

(Sec. 3) DOJ must coordinate with the Department of Health and Human Services to develop educational resources for mental health providers regarding the culture of law enforcement agencies and therapies for mental health issues common to law enforcement officers.

(Sec. 4) DOJ must also: (1) review existing crisis hotlines, recommend improvements, and research annual mental health checks; (2) examine the mental health and wellness needs of federal officers; (3) ensure that recommendations, resources, or programs under this bill protect the privacy of participating officers; and (4) report to Congress on findings and final recommendations.

summary.headline: This law asks the Justice Department to study and report on mental health support for police officers and lets some grant money fund peer mental health programs.
summary.what_it_does: The law directs the Department of Justice to look at mental health practices used by the military and Veterans Affairs to see whether police agencies could use them. It expands a federal police grant program so funds can pay for peer mentoring mental health pilot programs in state, local, and tribal police agencies. It also requires the Justice Department to work with Health and Human Services to create training materials for mental health providers about police culture and treatments for common officer issues. Finally, it requires reports on crisis hotlines, annual mental health checks, and the needs of federal officers, while protecting officers' privacy.

who_it_affects.group: State, local, and tribal law enforcement officers
who_it_affects.how: Their agencies may be able to get federal grant money for peer mentoring mental health and wellness pilot programs.

who_it_affects.group: State, local, and tribal police agencies
who_it_affects.how: They become eligible to use Community Oriented Policing Services grant funds for mental health and wellness pilot programs.
The Justice Department must review their mental health and wellness needs and protect the privacy of any officers who take part in related programs.
They may receive new educational resources on law enforcement culture and therapies for issues common to officers.
The Justice Department must review existing crisis hotlines and recommend improvements, though the law does not itself change how hotlines operate.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was enacted on January 10, 2018, but its reporting and program provisions depend on later agency action and funding.
